text: Kimberley (Khoekhoe: ǃ’Ās; Tswana: Kimbali) is the capital and largest city of the Northern Cape province of South Africa, located approximately 110 km east of the confluence of the Vaal and Orange Rivers. It holds significant historical importance due to its diamond mining heritage and the siege during the Second Boer War. British businessmen Cecil Rhodes and Barney Barnato built their fortunes in Kimberley, with Rhodes founding the De Beers diamond company in the early days of the mining town. On 2 September 1882, Kimberley became the first city in the Southern Hemisphere and the second in the world after Philadelphia, United States, to install electric street lighting. The first stock exchange in Africa, the Kimberley Royal Stock Exchange, opened on 2 February 1881. In 1866, Erasmus Jacobs found a 21.25-carat (4.3 g) diamond on the Orange River near Hopetown, which became known as the Eureka; it was purchased by Schalk van Niekerk and later sold. In 1869, an 83.5-carat (16.7 g) diamond, known as the Star of South Africa, was found nearby (29°3′S 23°58′E﻿ / ﻿29.050°S 23.967°E﻿ / -29.050; 23.967), sold by van Niekerk for £11,200 and later resold in London for £25,000. In 1871, Esau Damoense, the cook for prospector Fleetwood Rawstorne's "Red Cap Party", found diamonds on Colesberg Kopje, prompting Rawstorne to inform the De Beer brothers, sparking the "New Rush" with 900 claims and two to three thousand miners working the area, which eventually became the world-renowned Kimberley Mine. The Cape Colony, Transvaal, Orange Free State, and Griqua leader Nicolaas Waterboer all claimed the diamond fields, with the Free State Boers wanting the area due to its location within the Orange and Vaal River borders. After mediation by the Governor of Natal, the Keate Award favored Waterboer, who placed himself under British protection, leading to the proclamation of Griqualand West on 27 October 1871. Colonial Commissioners arrived in New Rush on 17 November 1871, and Governor Barkly visited in September 1872, proposing to make Griqualand West a Crown Colony. Richard Southey arrived as Lieutenant-Governor in January 1873, but delays in London, where Secretary of State for the Colonies John Wodehouse, 1st Earl of Kimberley, insisted on "decent and intelligible names" and rejected "New Rush" and "Vooruitzigt", led to a renaming. Colonial Secretary J.B. Currey renamed the area "Kimberley" by proclamation dated 5 July 1873, a move that was criticized in an editorial in the Diamond Field newspaper, which stated, "we went to sleep in New Rush and waked up in Kimberley, and so our dream was gone". After British government compensation to the Orange Free State, Griqualand West was annexed to the Cape Colony in 1877. Cape Prime Minister John Molteno initially opposed annexation due to financial concerns but passed the Griqualand West Annexation Act on 27 July 1877 after securing assurances of local consultation. From mid-July 1871 to 1914, 50,000 miners dug the Big Hole (or Kimberley se Gat in Afrikaans), which has a surface of 17 hectares (42 acres), is 463 metres wide, was excavated to 240 metres in depth, partially infilled to about 215 metres, and now has 40 metres of water, leaving 175 metres visible; beneath it, the Kimberley Mine was mined to 1097 metres. The Big Hole is the principal feature of a 2004 submission placing "Kimberley Mines and associated early industries" on UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative Lists. By 1873, Kimberley was the second-largest town in South Africa with a population of approximately 40,000. Smaller mining companies were amalgamated by Cecil Rhodes and Charles Rudd into De Beers and by Barney Barnato into The Kimberley, and in 1888, the two merged to form De Beers Consolidated Mines, which held a monopoly over the world's diamond market. The city grew rapidly due to a large African migration seeking cheap labour from the De Beers company, and also attracted prostitutes from various ethnicities, earning a reputation as a city of limitless opportunity. Five big holes were dug into kimberlite pipes, named after the town; the largest, the Kimberley Mine or "Big Hole", covering 170,000 square metres (42 acres), reached a depth of 240 metres (790 ft) and yielded three tons of diamonds, closing in 1914, while Dutoitspan, Wesselton, and Bultfontein closed in 2005. On 14 October 1899, Kimberley was besieged at the start of the Second Boer War, with British relief forces suffering heavy losses; the siege ended on 15 February 1900, though the war continued until May 1902, during which British forces established a concentration camp for Boer women and children. The Boroughs of Kimberley and Beaconsfield amalgamated into the City of Kimberley in 1912. Urban segregation existed before apartheid, and the Group Areas Act enforced racial separation into European (White), Native (Black), Coloured, and Indian categories, with families split by measures like the 'pencil test' and communities relocated (e.g., Malay Camp) or selectively cleared (e.g., Greenpoint). New townships were created at the city's northern and north-eastern edges, and institutions like churches (e.g., Bean Street Methodist Church) and schools (e.g., William Pescod and Perseverance School) were affected, with some closing or relocating. The Reservation of Separate Amenities Act restricted African movement and designated public places as 'Europeans Only', and the Native Laws Amendment Act sought to divide church communities racially, a policy rejected by Archbishop Clayton in 1957. Resistance began in mid-1952 with the Defiance Campaign, when Dr Arthur Letele organized volunteers to occupy 'Europeans Only' benches at Kimberley Railway Station, leading to arrests; the Mayibuye Uprising on 8 November 1952, sparked by poor beer quality, resulted in shootings and a mass funeral on 12 November 1952, with detained leaders including Dr Letele, Sam Phakedi, Pepys Madibane, Olehile Sehume, Alexander Nkoane, Daniel Chabalala, and David Mpiwa. Archdeacon Wade of St Matthew's Church blamed apartheid policies, including poor housing, lighting, and transport, and unfulfilled promises, for the riots. Later anti-apartheid activists in Kimberley included Phakamile Mabija, Bishop Graham Chadwick, and provincial premiers Manne Dipico and Dipuo Peters. Prominent figures with Kimberley connections include Robert Sobukwe, founder of the Pan Africanist Congress, who was banished to the city after release from Robben Island in 1969 and died there in 1978; Benny Alexander (1955–2010), who later changed his name to Khoisan X and served as General Secretary of the Pan Africanist Congress and Pan-Africanist Movement from 1989, was born and raised in Kimberley. The Northern Cape Province became a political reality in 1994 with Kimberley as its capital; infrastructure existed since the 1940s, but post-1994 development included administrative departments, a Northern Cape Legislature, and an enlarged Kimberley City Council, now the Sol Plaatje Local Municipality, named after the prominent writer and activist who lived in the area. The former Diamantveld District Council became the Frances Baard District Municipality, named after the trade unionist born in Greenpoint, Kimberley. The Kimberley borough council adopted a coat of arms in 1878, registered with the Cape Provincial Administration in December 1964 and the Bureau of Heraldry in February 1968; the design combined the Union Jack with elements of the Cape Colony's coat of arms and a lozenge symbolizing the diamond industry: Azure, a cross and saltire superimposed Gules, both fimbriated Argent, in chief three bezants Or, each charged with a fleur de lis Azure, and in base three annulets Or; on a lozenge Or, superimposed over the fess point, a lion rampant Gules. The motto was Spero meliora. The divisional council for rural areas registered its own arms in August 1970: Per saltire, in chief, barry wavy of six Argent and Azure; in base, Argent, a pale Sable charged with three fusils Argent; dexter, Gules, a shovel and pick in saltire, handles downward, Or; sinister, a staff of Aesculapius, Or. In layman's terms, the shield was divided diagonally with (1) six silver and blue wavy stripes, (2) a crossed pick and shovel on a red background, (3) a golden staff of Aesculapius, and (4) three silver diamond-shaped fusils on a black vertical stripe on a silver background. The crest featured two crossed rifles in front of an upright sword; the supporters were two kudus; the motto was "Nitanir semper ad optima". Kimberley was the initial hub of industrialization in late 19th-century South Africa, transforming the agrarian economy into one based on mineral wealth, with migrant labour becoming a key feature, especially in the mines. The city hosted South Africa's first school of mines, opened in 1896 and later relocated to Johannesburg, becoming the foundation of the University of the Witwatersrand, with a Pretoria campus later becoming the University of Pretoria. The first two years of the school were attended at colleges in Cape Town, Grahamstown, or Stellenbosch, with the third year in Kimberley.

Africa's first stock exchange, the Kimberley Royal Stock Exchange, opened on 2 February 1881. On 2 September 1882, Kimberley became the first town in the Southern Hemisphere to install electric street lighting, a feat previously achieved only by Philadelphia, in the United States. In 1892, the first South African and international exhibition was held in Kimberley, opened by Sir Henry Loch, Governor of the Cape of Good Hope, on 8 September, featuring art, paintings from Queen Victoria’s royal collection, mining machinery, and other exhibits, sparking international interest and leading to a competition for display space. South Africa's first school of mines opened in Kimberley in 1896 and later moved to Johannesburg, becoming the foundation of the University of the Witwatersrand; a Pretoria campus later evolved into the University of Pretoria. The first two years of study were completed in Cape Town, Grahamstown, or Stellenbosch, the third year in Kimberley, and the fourth in Johannesburg, with buildings constructed at a total cost of 9,000 pounds, funded on a pound-for-pound basis by De Beers. In 1913, Kimberley established South Africa's first school of aviation to train pilots for the proposed South African Aviation Corps (SAAC), known as Paterson's Aviation Syndicate School of Flying, now commemorated in the Pioneers of Aviation Museum with a replica of the first Compton Patterson Biplane. In the 1930s, Kimberley had the best night-landing facilities on the African continent, hosted a major air rally in 1934, and during wartime, Kimberley Airport was taken over by the Union Defence Force and operated by the 21 Flying School for fighter pilot training. Today, Kimberley Airport (IATA: KIM, ICAO: FAKM) serves the area with regular flights from Cape Town and Johannesburg. Rail connections to the Cape Colony’s coastline began in 1872 under the Cape Government Railways, with the Cape Town to Kimberley line completed in 1885, accelerating passenger and goods transport and linking Kimberley to cheaper grain and coal supplies, thereby undercutting local African trade in fresh produce and firewood; the railway also played a role in the rapid spread of the Spanish Influenza in 1918. The rail network eventually connected Kimberley to Port Elizabeth, Johannesburg, Durban, and Bloemfontein, with De Aar serving as a major junction linking to Upington (later Namibia) and Calvinia; rail use declined from the 1990s. Today, passenger services to and from Kimberley are operated by Spoornet’s Shosholoza Meyl, connecting south to Cape Town and Port Elizabeth and north to Johannesburg, with luxury services offered by the Blue Train and Rovos Rail; the central station is Kimberley railway station. Wagon and coach routes developed rapidly as diamond mining expanded, with major routes from the Cape and Port Elizabeth; accounts from the 1870s describe poor road conditions and a lack of bridges. From the mid-1880s, the route through Kimberley and Mafeking (now Mahikeng) became the main axis of British colonial expansion, from which the Pioneer Column set out in 1890 to settle Rhodesia. Today, the main north-south route, the N1, goes via Bloemfontein, not Kimberley. Kimberley lies at the intersection of the N12 and N8 national roads. It is the seat of the Northern Cape Provincial Legislature and Provincial Administration, serving the region’s mining and agricultural sectors. The city presents itself as a significant tourist destination, known as the 'City that Sparkles,' with diverse museums and attractions, and acts as a gateway to Northern Cape destinations such as Mokala National Park, nature reserves, game farms, hunting lodges, and historic sites. Kimberley has hosted major meetings, including the founding of the Kimberley Process in 2000 and a follow-up in 2013, and the International Indigenous Peoples Summit on Sustainable Development in 2002, with the Mittah Seperepere Convention Centre and other facilities supporting these events. Under the Köppen system, Kimberley has a semi-arid climate (BSh) with long, wet summers and short, mild, dry winters with chilly nights. Water is drawn from the Vaal River at Riverton, about 15 km north of the city. According to the 2011 census, the population of Kimberley "proper" was 96,977, with Galeshewe and Roodepan having populations of 107,920 and 20,263 respectively, giving an urban total of 225,160; 63.1% identified as Black African, 26.8% as Coloured, 8.0% as White, and 1.2% as Indian or Asian; 43.2% spoke Afrikaans, 35.8% Setswana, 8.7% English, 6.0% isiXhosa, and 2.7% Sesotho. The city lies on a flat landscape with no prominent topographic features, except for debris dumps from over a century of diamond mining, which have been recycled and filled back into De Beers Mine by 2010, with some near the Big Hole designated as heritage features. The surrounding rural area consists of flat plains with hills of andesite to the north and northwest, and Karoo-age dolerite to the south and east, forming shallow pans. A notable feature is Kamfers Dam, a large pan north of the city, an important wetland supporting a breeding colony of lesser flamingos; conservation efforts aim to engage city residents with local wildlife, though in 2012 rising water levels flooded an artificial island built to enhance flamingo breeding, and in December 2013 an outbreak of avian botulism killed hundreds of birds, after which the island re-emerged. The administration of the Crown Colony of Griqualand West (from 1873) was based in Kimberley’s Government Buildings until its annexation to the Cape in 1880. Separate Borough Councils in Kimberley and Beaconsfield operated until their amalgamation into the City of Kimberley in 1912, after which a single City Council governed the city and a Divisional Council managed the rural district; in the 1980s, a separate political entity called Galeshewe (with Mankurwane) was created with its own council. Post-1994, the Kimberley City Council became the Sol Plaatje Local Municipality, and the successor to the Diamandveld Regional Services Council became the Frances Baard District Municipality. The idea of the Northern Cape as a distinct geographic entity began in the 1940s but became official in 1994, with Kimberley designated as the province’s legislative capital; the provincial legislature initially used the old Cape Provincial Administration building before moving to a purpose-built facility between a township and former white suburbs. Kimberley is also the seat of the Northern Cape Division of the High Court of South Africa. Education is a key sector in Kimberley’s social and economic life. Sol Plaatje University opened in Kimberley in 2014 with an initial intake of 135 students; former President Jacob Zuma highlighted its focus on heritage studies, including museum management, archaeology, indigenous languages, and restoration architecture. Former tertiary institutions in Kimberley have been absorbed into these structures. The city has historically attracted diverse faith communities, including various Christian denominations, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, and traditional African beliefs, notably in the Zionist Christian Church (ZCC); it is the seat of the Anglican Diocese of Kimberley and Kuruman and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kimberley (formerly the Apostolic Vicariate of Kimberley in Orange), with churches also belonging to the Methodist Church, Presbyterian Church, Congregational Church, Dutch Reformed Church, Baptist Church, Afrikaans Baptist Church, Apostolics, Pentecostals, and the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Notable artists include William Timlin, Walter Westbrook, and Philip Bawcombe. Writers from Kimberley or with strong ties include Diane Awerbuck, Benjamin Bennett, Lawrence Green, Dorian Haarhoff, Dan Jacobson, E P Lekhela, Z.K. Matthews, Sarah Gertrude Millin, Sol Plaatje, Frank Templeton Prince, Olive Schreiner, A.H.M. Scholtz, and Sabata-Mpho Mokae. Dr Victor is a notable reggae and rhythm and blues musician from the city. Memorials include the Diamond Field, the first newspaper published on 15 October 1870 at Pniel; other early papers were the Diamond News and the Independent; the current daily is the Diamond Fields Advertiser, first published on 23 March 1878. The Volksblad, with a free local supplement called Noordkaap, is read by Afrikaans-speaking residents. Two community radio stations were established in the 1990s. Kimberley has contributed significantly to cricket history, producing international players such as Frank (Nipper) Nicholson, Xenophon Balaskas (born to Greek parents), Ken Viljoen, Ronnie Draper, Pat Symcox, and coach Mickey Arthur; it hosted a match during the 2003 ICC Cricket World Cup, and Elsie McDonald was a Springbok bowler. Frank Dobbin, known as Uncle Dobbin, was part of Paul Roos’ original Springboks on the 1906/1907 tour to the British Isles; his memory is preserved in his colonial-style home in Roper Street with a brass plaque. Later Springboks to wear green and gold included Ian Kirkpatrick, Tommy Bedford, and Gawie Visagie, brother of Piet Visagie of Ammosal. Kimberley is home to the Griquas rugby team, which won the Currie Cup in 1899, 1911, 1970, and 2025; Ronnie Bauser, an ex-mayor of Kimberley, was involved with the team from 1950 to 1971. Richard Henyekane, a South African footballer, is from Kimberley, as is his younger brother Joseph, who played for Golden Arrows; Jimmy Tau is also from the city. Karen Muir, born in Kimberley, became in 1965 the youngest person to break a world record in any sport at age 12, setting the record in the 110-metre backstroke at the junior world championships in Blackpool, England; the record still stands. She was denied a spot at the 1968 Olympics due to South Africa’s apartheid policies. A world record was also broken in the municipal pool named after her, beaten by Johannesburg’s Anne Fairlie and Frances Kikki Caron. Charl Bouwer, the Paralympic swimmer who won gold in the 50m freestyle at the 2012 London Paralympics, was born in Kimberley. Bevil Rudd is an Olympic medallist. The first Maloof Money Cup World Skateboarding Championships were held in Kimberley in September 2011 and again in 2012; after the Maloof sponsorship ended in 2013, the event became known as the Kimberley Diamond Cup. H.F. Oppenheimer, in a 1976 foreword, stated that the discovery of diamonds in Kimberley was the first step in transforming South Africa from an agricultural to an industrial nation, noting that when gold and other minerals were later found to the north, Kimberley already had men of vision and enterprise with the capital and technology to develop them. Anthony Trollope visited Kimberley in 1877 and was deeply unimpressed by the heat, dust, and flies, remarking that the people were proud of their flies and dust and describing the town as having only one building with a storey above ground, no pavement, and an ugly market place surrounded by corrugated iron shops. A.H.J. Bourne, former headmaster of Kimberley Boys' High School, observed in 1937 that Kimberley’s rapid growth from a bare veld suggested a supermind behind its development. In the early 1990s, writer Dan Jacobson returned to Kimberley, where he had grown up in the 1930s, noting that the people and their language had vanished, and that Afrikaans had replaced English as the common language among whites, blacks, and Coloureds. Virtualtourist reviewer Catherine Reichardt asked if Kimberley was dull, and responded that the answer is a resounding 'No' for those passionate about history, as the city offers rich historical depth and is best appreciated with an overnight stay, providing a microcosm of South African history.
